Y otros más anómalos o menos estudiados, como los niños que recuerdan vidas pasadas o las llamadas experiencias cercanas a la muerte (ECM): episodios intensos que algunas personas relatan tras superar una situación de muerte, como salir del propio cuerpo, atravesar un túnel o ver una luz intensa.

Más información La izquierda debe prestar atención a la búsqueda de respuesta de los jóvenes en la religión

El estudio de estos fenómenos no es nuevo. Las ECM se investigan desde los años setenta, a partir de los trabajos del psiquiatra Raymond Moody, y hace décadas que el también psiquiatra Ian Stevenson documentó supuestos recuerdos de vidas pasadas que apuntalarían la reencarnación. Ahora vivimos un boom, seguramente ligado a un repunte general de la espiritualidad, que ha multiplicado las obras sobre estos temas y vuelve virales a sus autores cada vez que pasan por un podcast. No todos son outsiders: entre sus valedores hay investigadores de primera fila, como el cardiólogo Valentín Fuster, premio Príncipe de Asturias de Investigación Científica y Técnica, que prologa Ego y supraconciencia (Planeta, 2025), del cirujano Manuel Sans Segarra, con una destacada trayectoria en el Hospital Universitario de Bellvitge. O Robert W. Wilson, Nobel de Física por descubrir la radiación de fondo que confirmó el Big Bang, que firma el prólogo del libro de Bolloré y Bonnassies.

Uno de los precursores de esta última eclosión fue La prueba del cielo (2012), del neurocirujano estadounidense Eben Alexander, que ejerció 15 años en la Facultad de Medicina de Harvard. En noviembre de 2008, una meningitis bacteriana lo mantuvo una semana en coma; al despertar, relató lo que interpreta como un viaje real al más allá. Su testimonio reúne los rasgos que describen muchos pacientes: una experiencia extracorporal —salir del cuerpo y elevarse—, el encuentro con seres de luz o familiares fallecidos y una revisión instantánea pero minuciosa de la propia vida, todo envuelto en una lucidez, una paz y un amor de intensidad sin parangón.

Para Alexander, esta experiencia no puede ser una alucinación como la que inducen ciertas sustancias psicoactivas: sostiene que una vivencia de esa intensidad difícilmente podría generarse con áreas clave del cerebro inoperativas, como estaba el suyo durante el coma. Y añade que, a su juicio, hay diferencias claras entre una ECM —estructurada, persistente en la memoria y con efectos duraderos— y una alucinación, caótica y fragmentaria, que apenas deja rastro. “La vida después de la muerte ha sido probada más allá de toda duda desde una perspectiva científica. Lo que ocurre es que algunas personas no están lo suficientemente interesadas como para informarse”, sostiene el científico por videollamada.

Sin embargo, otros trabajos han cuestionado la interpretación de este fenómeno como prueba de una realidad trascendente. Uno de ellos es el estudio liderado por la neurocientífica Charlotte Martial, investigadora de la Universidad de Lieja, publicado el año pasado en Nature Reviews Neurology. En él, los autores proponen un modelo que integra décadas de investigación y explica las ECM como el resultado de una cascada de procesos neurobiológicos en un cerebro sometido a estrés extremo. Factores como la falta de oxígeno, el aumento de dióxido de carbono y las alteraciones en la actividad eléctrica cerebral desencadenan una hiperactividad neuronal y una liberación masiva de neurotransmisores capaces de generar experiencias intensas, coherentes y emocionalmente profundas.

Más allá de este experimento, uno de los problemas para estudiar las ECM, y otros fenómenos trascendentes, es que ocurren en una dimensión inmaterial, fuera del espacio y del tiempo. Eso las sitúa fuera del alcance de las herramientas de la ciencia. El método científico se basa en fenómenos que pueden observarse, medirse y reproducirse. “Podríamos demostrar que esas personas han visto algo, no que ese algo estuviera ahí de verdad”, explica por teléfono el filósofo Carlos Blanco, autor de Conciencia y mismidad (Dykinson, 2013). Que algo no se pueda observar, matiza, no implica que no exista: “Una cosa es el orden del ser y otra el del conocer”.

Parte de la ciencia se basa en inferir causas no observables a partir de mediciones indirectas. Ocurre, por ejemplo, con los electrones, que no vemos directamente, sino a través de sus efectos, o con los agujeros negros, cuya existencia se deduce por cómo afectan a la materia y la luz a su alrededor. Pero hay una diferencia fundamental, explica el filósofo de la ciencia Óscar Teixidó: los electrones o los agujeros negros no se observan directamente, pero dejan huellas medibles y consistentes en la materia. En cambio, una conciencia fuera del espacio-tiempo no deja rastro alguno. “Ya no solo es que sea inobservable, sino que además está en otro plano de existencia”, afirma.

Blanco afirma que algunas de las supuestas pruebas científicas de la existencia de Dios son un regreso a viejos argumentos filosóficos. El razonamiento parte de un efecto observable —que el universo tiene leyes, orden, unas constantes tan ajustadas que parecen preparadas para acoger la vida— y retrocede desde él hasta una causa, Dios, como hizo Tomás de Aquino. Pero del efecto, argumenta Blanco, no se puede deducir la causa: se incurre en lo que en lógica se llama falacia de afirmación del consecuente.

Un mismo efecto admite explicaciones distintas, y nada en la mera observación permite decidir cuál es la verdadera. “Todo podría ser fruto del azar, o de que el universo sea simplemente así, eterno, o de que existan otros universos, multiversos. Dios es una causa posible, por supuesto, pero hay otras. ¿Cómo decides cuál es la correcta si no hay observaciones ni experimentos?”, plantea.

Otra de las grandes críticas es la del rigor experimental y la necesidad de aplicar estándares metodológicos suficientemente exigentes. Según Teixidó, en los últimos años se ha producido un “retroceso intelectual” que ha hecho olvidar principios básicos ya asentados: evitar sesgos, desconfiar de la evidencia anecdótica y no dejarse arrastrar por creencias previas: “El problema es que no se están aplicando filtros de rigor realmente exhaustivos. Cuando uno es exigente, muchas de estas investigaciones se reducen a tres cosas: confusiones inocentes, errores deliberados o simples mitos. Es humo”.

En el otro lado, Álex Gómez-Marín, investigador sénior del Instituto de Neurociencias y científico titular del CSIC, que ha contado la ECM que vivió en su libro La ciencia del último umbral (Temas de Hoy, 2025), sostiene que quienes cuestionan su falta de rigor experimental, en realidad, no están informados. “Este tipo de expertos siempre dicen, en nombre de la ciencia, que saben que no, cuando en realidad no saben. Y eso ha puesto muchas trabas en la investigación y ha hecho sentir tonta, loca y sola a mucha gente que experimenta estos fenómenos. Eso es poco científico y poco ético”.

Ante esta disputa, vale la pena recordar el prólogo que Albert Einstein escribió en 1930 para Mental Radio, un libro del escritor Upton Sinclair dedicado nada menos que a la telepatía. El padre de la relatividad no daba por buenos los experimentos de Sinclair; al contrario, los consideraba más allá de lo que un investigador de la naturaleza juzga pensable. Pero tampoco los descartaba: tenía a Sinclair por un observador escrupuloso, cuya “buena fe y fiabilidad no pueden ponerse en duda”, y razonaba que, si aquellos resultados no se debían a la telepatía, sino a algún influjo inconsciente de una mente sobre otra, el fenómeno seguiría siendo de gran interés psicológico. Ni credulidad ni rechazo: curiosidad y rigor.

World.title: Del ‘scroll’ infinito a volver con un ex: ¿por qué el cerebro nos hace repetir conductas que no queremos?
World.content:
No todo lo que parece que hacemos automáticamente es un hábito, muchas veces es una elección propia. Los expertos explican por qué el cerebro prioriza el alivio inmediato frente al bienestar futuro y qué papel tienen las emociones en el proceso

Cada día repetimos muchos comportamientos de forma inconsciente y hasta involuntaria. Desde pequeños automatismos, como levantarnos por la mañana y desbloquear el móvil o hábitos como tomar café a la misma hora, hasta otras formas recurrentes de actuar, como dejar tareas importantes para el último momento o procrastinar. Si bien algunos son comportamientos saludables y ayudan, otros son nocivos y nos complican la vida y, sin embargo, los seguimos repitiendo. ¿Por qué? ¿Qué hace que repitamos lo mismo una y otra vez a sabiendas que no nos hace bien? Para el psicólogo clínico y forense Aleix Hildebrandt, la explicación cómoda es que entramos en piloto automático y que el cerebro nos arrastra sin que podamos hacer nada. “Esta es una idea tranquilizadora, pero, en buena parte, es mentira”, asegura.

Según este especialista, más que preguntar por qué actuamos en modo automático habría que reflexionar si, en el fondo, es lo que elegimos e, incluso, lo que nuestro cerebro ha aprendido. “La pregunta es más incómoda: ¿y si muchas veces no estuviéramos en piloto automático, sino eligiendo, una y otra vez, el alivio de ahora por encima del bienestar de mañana?”, comenta Hildebrand. “Un hábito es una asociación entre un contexto y una respuesta que se dispara sola con un coste mental mínimo, y que se ha vuelto casi indiferente a si todavía quieres el resultado, como coger el móvil en cuanto notas el bolsillo vibrar, encenderse un cigarro al salir del portal o morderse una uña cuando lees un correo tenso. Son gestos, no decisiones y te descubres haciéndolos”, comenta.

Un patrón de comportamiento, en cambio, es otra cosa mucho más amplia. “Incluye emociones, pensamientos, motivos y, muchas veces, a otras personas. Volver con quien te hace daño no es un hábito, es un patrón donde conviven el apego, el miedo a la soledad, la recompensa intermitente, esos días buenos que lo justifican todo, y toda una biografía”, explica el experto. Llamar “hábito” a volver con tu ex es como llamar “costumbre” a una herida que no cierra, según él: “Cabe en la misma frase, pero no es lo mismo, y tratarlo como un simple automatismo garantiza que no lo entiendes”.

El reciente estudio El comportamiento y los hábitos humanos, publicado en la plataforma Open Science Framework y llevado a cabo por investigadores españoles, analizó los principales protocolos sobre la formación de hábitos en humanos, y ha concluido que estos protocolos presentan limitaciones para demostrar que los comportamientos observados están realmente guiados por hábitos automáticos y no por procesos deliberativos. “Los hábitos empiezan como decisiones conscientes, pero la repetición constante en un mismo contexto hace que el cerebro automatice progresivamente esa conducta”, explica a EL PAIS Pablo Martínez, psicólogo experto en neurociencia cognitiva y conductual y uno de los autores principales del estudio.

Cada día repetimos muchos comportamientos de forma inconsciente y hasta involuntaria, desde pequeños automatismos como levantarnos por la mañana y desbloquear el móvil. Fiordaliso (Getty Images)

Aunque solemos pensar que muchos comportamientos son completamente automáticos, la evidencia científica sugiere que la frontera entre las decisiones conscientes y los hábitos es más difusa de lo que parece. “Cuando no tenemos suficientes recursos cognitivos para evaluar cuál es la mejor conducta o decisión, nuestro cerebro dispara lo que había hecho anteriormente, porque seguramente eso era lo correcto o lo recompensado. Esto permite una gran adaptación si los hábitos que tenemos consolidados son adaptativos, pues seguramente estén alineados con nuestras metas y objetivos en ese momento”, argumenta Martínez. “Son conductas que hemos realizado muy a menudo en el pasado y el sistema neurocognitivo que los sustenta es permeable, por lo que son respuestas que se activan dados ciertos contextos”, prosigue David Luque, psicólogo investigador en neurociencia cognitiva y otro de los autores de la investigación.

Algunos ‘malos hábitos’ son intentos de regulación emocional

Rosa Molina, psiquiatra experta en salud y bienestar vinculada al estudio Bienestar Extendido 2040 de Espacio Futuro —que pone de manifiesto que la salud se ha convertido en una experiencia cada vez más condicionada por factores como el estrés sostenido, la falta de tiempo o la inseguridad económica—, asegura que muchas conductas que se etiquetan como “malos hábitos” son en realidad intentos de regulación emocional o nuestro termómetro emocional. “Mirar repetidamente el móvil o hacer scroll en redes sociales, procrastinar o volver a una relación dañina pueden proporcionar alivio inmediato frente al estrés, la ansiedad o la soledad”, sostiene esta experta.

Además, destaca un matiz importante que se desprende de la investigación sobre hábitos del Open Science. “La idea del estudio de que no siempre lo que llamamos ‘hábito automático’ es realmente un hábito en sentido estricto es cierta. La neurociencia experimental nos recuerda que muchas de estas conductas repetidas pueden estar más guiadas por la búsqueda de alivio emocional inmediato que por una automatización genuina del comportamiento”, asevera Molina.

Cuando una persona dice: “Sé que esto me hace daño, pero lo sigo haciendo”, estamos simplificando demasiado lo que ocurre en el cerebro. “Solemos pensar que saber algo debería bastar para cambiarlo, pero el cerebro no funciona así. La persona sabe perfectamente lo que le conviene, pero el problema es que aquello que racionalmente considera importante compite con señales que el cerebro ha aprendido a etiquetar como muy relevantes. El conocimiento compite con sistemas mucho más antiguos y complejos relacionados con la recompensa, el alivio emocional y la supervivencia”, explica Molina.

"Entender por qué fumas no apaga el cigarro, es decir, ese 'insight' informa, pero no ejecuta”, explica el psicólogo clínico y forense Aleix Hildebrandt. SimpleImages (Getty Images)

Hildebrandt recuerda que entender y hacer viven en sitios distintos del cerebro. “El conocimiento de que algo es malo es información; la conducta se ejecuta en un sistema mucho más ligado a la emoción y a la recompensa, y ese sistema no lee informes. Entender por qué fumas no apaga el cigarro, es decir, ese insight informa, pero no ejecuta”, espeta. “Además, el cerebro no distingue bien entre lo que te conviene y lo que te calma. Y en el momento decisivo casi siempre gana lo que te calma, no es un automatismo ciego, es un pulso entre dos relojes que marcan horas distintas”, expresa el experto.

“Los hábitos son más difíciles de controlar cuando estamos en situación de estrés, estamos cansados o tenemos que reaccionar muy rápidamente”, advierte Martínez. Y añade: “Son condiciones donde nuestros recursos cognitivos están disminuidos y eso hace que lo que se activa por defecto, que es el hábito, no lo podamos controlar”.

World.title: Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
World.content:
More than 500 people have joined a campaign to stop a huge data centre being built in Amsterdam-Zuid, arguing that it will bring “zero benefits to the area”.

The Dutch government has introduced restrictions on the size of data centres in recent years following criticism from provincial and municipal governments about the strain on the electricity network. Data centres accounted for 4.6% of all electricity use in the Netherlands in 2024.

But the plans to build a 24,000 m2 facility on Amsterdam’s Science Park were submitted by US firm Equinix before the ban, which only applies to new developments, took effect in 2022.

Local residents have also become increasingly vocal in opposing the construction of data centres, while campaign groups Geef Tegengas and Extinction Rebellion both staged demonstrations this summer against a Microsoft project in Amsterdam Sloterdijk.

“There are already enough data centres to keep everything running. This is becoming overkill,” Dylan Bakker of Stop Datacenter Zuidoost told NOS.

Amsterdam city council, which wants to build 8,000 homes in Zuidoost to help relieve the national housing shortage, has attached extra conditions to the site, such as requiring the residual heat from the plant to be used for domestic heating.

Water and electricity

There are also concerns about the strain on water supplies, which have been exacerbated by the summer drought. Equinix said in its planning application that it would need 274 million litres of water a year for the first stage of the project, rising to more than a billion litres when the data centre is complete in 2036.

But the municipality says it would face legal action and penalties if it tore up the permit to build the data center at this stage.

Equinix has said it will only build one of four planned 60-metre data towers initially, until electricity grid operator Tennet can supply enough power.

Tennet warned earlier this year that the network was nearing capacity, leading to a six-month moratorium on new connections in Utrecht.

The complete campus in Zuidoost will consume 779 kWh of electricity a year, almost as much as all the households Amsterdam combined, which currently use 869 kWh.

Michiel Eielts, director of Equinix Benelux, argued that the data centres were an essential part of modern infrastructure. “Every house needs the internet. We need data centres for the growth of our companies, our public services and our security,” he said.

World.title: Dutch men face Argentina in World Cup hockey, women win again
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch men’s hockey team are taking on Argentina in their second World Cup group match on Tuesday, with the winners set to take a giant step towards the knock-out rounds.

Both teams won their opening matches comfortably, with the Netherlands beating New Zealand 5-1 in Amstelveen while Argentina overcame Japan by a 3-0 scoreline at the same venue.

The Netherlands and Belgium are co-hosting the tournament, 12 years after the World Cup was held in The Hague. On that occasion the Dutch women’s team won their tournament while the men lost in the final to Australia.

The women’s team are on the brink of reaching the quarter-finals this time after coming through a tricky tie against Australia to win 4-2.

Goalkeeper Anne Veenendaal was kept busy in the opening period as the Dutch had to defend seven penalty corners before taking the lead when Yibbi Jansen scored from a penalty corner at the other end.

Joosje Burg made it two midway through the second period, but Australia hit back almost immediately through Stephanie Kershaw.

After a goalless third quarter, the Australians equalised when Abigail Wilson converted a penalty corner, but Burg restored the lead with her second before Marijn Veen rounded off a fine move to make sure of the points.

In an intriguing subplot, the Argentinian men’s team includes Nicolas Keenan, the fiancé of Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by hockey.nl (@hockeynl)



Jetten wore an Argentina replica shirt as he cheered on his partner from the sidelines on Sunday’s match, but was evasive when asked by RTL which team he would be supporting on Tuesday.

“Hopefully it’ll be a draw so we don’t have to fall out at home,” he joked.

World.title: More Dutch adults are single or living apart, says CBS
World.content:
The amount of people in the Netherlands who are single is rising, and a growing number are in relationships with a partner they do not live with, new figures from statistics agency CBS show.

In 2025, 30% of adults said they had no long-term partner, up from 27% in 2013. A further 10% were in a so-called “living apart together” relationship – a couple who keep separate homes – compared with 8% in 2013. The remaining 60% lived with a partner.

At the start of 2025, 5.7 million adults did not live with a partner. Most of them, 4.4 million, were living alone, while 627,000 were single parents and others still lived with their own parents.

Single women happier

Single women were more likely to call themselves happy (82%) than single men (76%), the agency found. People in couples were happier still: 92% of those living with a partner said they were happy, whether married or not.

Women were slightly more likely to be single overall (32%) than men (28%). Among the under-25s, most were single (62%) or living apart from a partner (29%), and just 8% shared a home with one.

The pattern shifts with age. From 45 onwards single women outnumber single men, an effect CBS links partly to divorce, after which men more often find a new partner. Among divorced women, 68% were single, against 55% of divorced men.

By 75 and over, about 42% of people lived alone with no partner, mostly because a partner had died. Just over half were still living with someone.

World.title: Schools return as new Dutch and maths targets become law
World.content:
Schools in the north of the Netherlands are the first to go back after the summer holidays, and they return to a new set of legally binding targets for what pupils have to learn in Dutch and maths.

The updated core curriculum objectives (kerndoelen) were written into law this month for the first time, NOS reported on Monday. They set out the knowledge and skills pupils are expected to acquire in primary school and the first years of secondary education.

The previous objectives dated from 2006 and were criticised as out of date, vague, and non-committal. There are now fewer of them for Dutch, but what pupils should be able to do is described more concretely. Literature has a clearly defined role, and language development is to be built into other subjects as well.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen said the change was needed because of a serious decline in basic language and maths skills.

Falling standards

The Netherlands was previously seen internationally as one of the leaders in reading, but standards have dropped sharply in recent years.

Tielen wrote to MPs recently that no other European country has seen learning performance fall as far, and school inspectors have found year after year that many children cannot read, write, or do basic maths at the expected level.

Earlier attempts to turn this around – a masterplan on basic skills launched in 2022 and the national programme set up to make up for learning lost during the coronavirus closures – have not had the intended effect, Tielen said. She is working on a new approach prioritising language.

The objectives for the remaining subjects, including two new ones – digital literacy and citizenship – are due to be made law next summer. Schools have until 2031 to incorporate all of them into their teaching.

Ilja Cornelisz, an education researcher at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, said ambitious objectives do matter because basic skills are under pressure, but that more is needed to improve schooling.

The real task, he said, is giving teachers the professional room, the reliable knowledge, and the support to deliver the goals in their own classrooms, while leaving schools free to decide how they get there.

World.title: Two minors held after second Zaandam explosion in five days
World.content:
Police have arrested two minors on suspicion of involvement in an explosion that blew the back wall off a Zaandam flat in the early hours of Monday.

The blast at the Hof van Zaenden was reported at about 1.40am and was followed by a fire, which the fire service put out quickly. Residents of the block were evacuated because of fears it might collapse, regional broadcaster NH reported.

Nobody was in the flat where the device went off and no one was hurt by the blast, police said.

Officers found the two suspects in a car close to the block shortly after the explosion. Police have not given their ages, saying only that both are under 18.

Debris from the wall was scattered on both sides of the building, and windows and frames in neighbouring flats were damaged. Forensic officers worked with the defence ministry’s bomb disposal unit to secure evidence at the scene.

It is the second explosion in Zaandam in five days. A blast damaged a window at a house on Saenredamstraat late on Thursday, and police are still appealing for witnesses.

World.title: The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?
World.content:
The IamExpat Fair returns to Eindhoven on Saturday October 3 for its second outing in the city, with a bigger careers section, two international centres and a new kids area.

The fair, which takes place in the Klokgebouw in Strijp-S, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, including special offers only available for attendees. You can register for free online.

“We are bringing back the large career section, expanding the number of expat centres at the fair, and growing the Family & Kids section,” says event manager Claire Leunissen.

Workshops and presentations

The fair will also feature over 20 free workshops to help expats with job hunting, finding housing, immigration and settling advice, as well as tips on local leisure and health services, and more. The workshops have limited capacity and are filling up fast, so make sure to book seats as soon as possible — you can sign up here.

Careers and partners

The careers section includes Brainport and recruitment agency Undutchables, and offers additional advice and services for the partners of people who have moved to the region for work.

“The international community of Eindhoven can’t be underestimated,” says Claire. “Because of this small but mighty community, we are bringing the Fair back to Eindhoven to support internationals and their families looking to to settle into Dutch life as well, through career opportunities, community groups, fitness schools, Dutch classes, and more.”

Families and newcomers

New this year is a kids area, supervised by childcare provider Korein, where families can play while parents work their way round the stands.

Two international centres will be on hand for questions about registration and residency: Holland Expat Center South, based in Eindhoven, and Expat Centre Maastricht Region. Orion Immigration Law returns with a stand double the size of last year’s.

Language schools include Language Institute Regina Coeli in Vught, Una Paloma Blanca, Bart de Pau and Taalkracht, while the health and leisure exhibitors range from bike subscription service Swapfiets to Happy Bodies and Shakti Nutrition.

Every stage covered

Workshops and presentations by experts run for most of the day, covering renting, buying a house and securing a mortgage, tax, careers and schooling.

“The fair is an incredible one-stop shop for every part of life in the Netherlands,” says Claire. “International students or young professionals may initially come to the Fair looking for Dutch language classes or career opportunities, but later in life, they come to the Fair for different needs, such as preparing for retirement, buying their first home, or choosing the right daycare for their kids.”

“We are excited to bring the IamExpat Fair back to the Klokgebouw, a historic building that embodies the history of technology, innovation and immigration of Eindhoven,” says Claire.

The IamExpat Fair Eindhoven takes place in the Klokgebouw, Strijp-S on Saturday October 3 from 10am to 5pm. Entrance is free with online registration.

World.title: Dutch destinations: Move on up to Midden-Groningen
World.content:
The area of countryside known as Midden-Groningen describes itself as the “playground” of the city of the same name. The region is home to country estates, windmills, little museums and plenty of outdoor places to explore by bike, foot and by boat.

Dotted around the countryside you will also see some of the traces of the regional gas industry, which has now been shut down because of the damage caused by earthquakes.

Five things to do in Midden-Groningen

Visit a country house

The Groningen country house, or borg, Fraeylemaborg in Slochteren was lived in by its wealthy owners well into the 20th century, but parts of the complex date back to the 13th. The entire building is now open to the public, from the attic to the kitchens and offers a fascinating glimpse into the lives of wealthy Groningers.

The grounds are also open to explore and regular re-enactments are staged in the grounds. When we visited a medieval battle, complete with tents, villagers and cannon, was being re-created much to the delight of the many children in the audience. The café with its sunny terrace is a good stop for lunch.

Take in a museum

There are plenty of small, regional museums in the region. In Hoogezand you will find the national bus museum, which attracts bus fans from all over the globe, and a historic wharf that has been virtually untouched since 1922.

In Sappemeer is the fire brigade museum and your offspring will be able to help put out a fire on certain days in the summer. Zuidbroek is home to a railway museum, in the old station, with a treasure hunt, train simulator for budding drivers and a collection of model trains.

Check out a windmill

The region is home to several windmills, some of which were used to pump out water when the land was being drained. De Wachter, on the edge of Zuidlaren, is a working oilseed mill with a small museum and great views if you can brave the ladders to reach the top.

It still produces linseed and corn oil, and four types of spices, all of which you can buy in the shop. Open on Saturday and Wednesday afternoon.

Wander in nature

The Drentsche Aa national park, on the edge of Zuidlaren, takes its name from the river Aa which meanders through the countryside from Drenthe into Groningen province. Home to plenty of wildlife and megalithic tombs known as hunebedden, it is one of the oldest landscapes in the country. You can follow various cycling and walking routes and the visitors centre has a welcoming café for lunch or high tea.

See the Veenkoloniën by boat

Pick up a canoe or an electric motorboat at Peddel en zo in Kiel-Windeweer and follow one of several routes along canals and rivers, from one hour to a full day. You will pass through ribbon villages and the remains of old peat workings, with plenty of opportunities to stop for lunch or a swim.

Where to eat

There is plenty of choice throughout the region. De Amshoff in Kiel-Windeweer comes highly recommended for dinner but was fully booked when we were there. It also offers overnight stays. Van Heijningen Bosch in Veendam is housed in a listed country house and serves lunch and evening fine dining.

The Grand Café in Zuidlaren offers traditional Dutch café fare – steaks, spare ribs – as well as cheese fondue and a hearty Dutch stew. Be aware, many places are closed Monday, Tuesday and even Wednesday, so check first.

Where to stay

We stayed in a little wooden cabin in the small-scale complex known as Romala’s Home in Kiel-Windeweer, where they also have a fascinating (enormous) shop full of bric-a-brac.

Het Torentje van Trips is a B&B in a converted water mill which sleeps up to eight in the east of the region. Zuidlaren has a couple of fairly ordinary hotels while Pieks in Noordlaren gets rave reviews online. There are also plenty of campsites if you are looking for something a little less refined.

How to get there

There are some bus and train services, but a car is probably the best, and easiest, way to get around. Rent a bike if you like cycling.

Anything else?

If you are looking for a longer stay, there is plenty more to explore in north eastern Groningen, including the fortified village of Bourtange and lots more borgs (manor houses).

World.title: Warning after Dutch blood donor infected with West Nile virus
World.content:
A case of West Nile virus has been detected in a Dutch blood donor in the first infection of its kind for six years.

The donor, who lives in Utrecht province, is though to have contracted the virus in the Netherlands, as they have not been abroad recently, the public health agency RIVM said.

The virus was confirmed after the patient reported mild symptoms of West Nile fever. Blood bank Sanquin subsequently carried out laboratory tests on a number of samples.

Some 80% of people who contract the virus have no symptoms, but around 1% develop neurological problems, mainly people over 50 with weakened immune systems. In rare cases it can be fatal.

The disease mainly occurs in birds, but can be transmitted to other species, including humans, by mosquitoes. There are no known cases of transmission between humans.

Horse and bird infected

The RIVM said the virus had also been detected in a horse and a bird in different locations in the Netherlands, indicating that mosquitoes that carry the virus are active in the country.

The agency advised people to wear clothes with long sleeves, apply mosquito repellent and use screens or mosquito nets to keep the insects out. It added that the risk of contracting West Nile virus in the Netherlands was small.

World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. The proportion of children taking Catholic catechism in schools has continued to fall but remains a majority https://t.co/5bu35hzJ7c — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. World.title: Poland seeks to boost investment with new tax-free personal accounts
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) without paying capital gains tax. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. To największa od lat zmiana dla indywidualnych inwestorów i największy projekt budowy krajowego kapitału napędzającego rozwój polskiej gospodarki. 🇵🇱 — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) July 3, 2026 The government estimates the scheme could result in about 74 billion zloty flowing to the Warsaw Stock Exchange by 2040. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. Poland’s WIG20 stock market index has hit its highest ever level, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year, gaining almost 25% https://t.co/CBbv99v2Uk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Poland already has three mechanisms that allow people to accumulate assets with tax advantages: Individual Retirement Accounts (IKE), Individual Pension Schemes (IKZE), and Employee Capital Plans (PPK). However, in all three cases, the capital gains tax exemption is conditional on withdrawing funds after reaching retirement age. Despite the Polish stock market’s strong performance in recent years, Poles’ direct participation remains modest. Shares make up only 2.9% of household assets, the equivalent of 3% of GDP. That is well below the EU average of 8.2%. By contrast, households’ cash holdings are equivalent to 11.5% of GDP, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). World.title: Polish PM confirms he wants his “right-hand man” to be made constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and whom Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. A newly sworn-in @TK_GOV_PL judge says he will not take his seat until four colleagues appointed by parliament are allowed to take theirs. He said their appointments had been blocked "unlawfully", in the latest twist in a long-running disputehttps://t.co/X30rm1Gfzs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 However, there remain major potential stumbling blocks on Berek’s path to the TK, not least doubts over whether Tusk’s coalition partners will support his nomination in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, declared on Tuesday that, if rumours of Berek’s nomination were true, “he won’t get votes from The Left because we promised our voters that politicians wouldn’t end up on the TK”. Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition to oppose Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. On Thursday, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK. Ale IMHO to bardzo krzywdząca dla @MaciejBerek plotka, on by się jako państwowiec w życiu na coś takiego nie… https://t.co/QWFFmdy4V3 — Anna-Maria Żukowska 💁🏻‍♀️ (@AM_Zukowska) August 11, 2026 The next vacancy on the TK’s 15-judge bench is due to open on 18 September, when the nine-year term of Justyn Piskorski, one of the PiS-era judges regarded as illegitimate by the current government, ends. After that, a further vacancy will open in January. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Earlier this week, his chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Radio Zet that Nawrocki would “accept the oath if procedures are followed”. However, he added that he does “not know if [the Sejm] is able to carry out those procedures properly”. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the reintroduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices. World.title: Poland says it foiled Russian plot to “execute” US-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained a Russian national who it says was planning to assassinate a person with joint US and Ukrainian citizenship in Warsaw. The news was first announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a press conference on Thursday afternoon. “Thanks to the truly brilliant action of our security services – the Internal Security Agency (ABW) with the assistance of the police – on 7 August we detained a Russian citizen, recruited by Russian intelligence services, whose task was to execute an American and Ukrainian citizen right here in Warsaw,” he said. “This is the first time someone on Russian orders has decided to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country,” added Tusk. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: 7 sierpnia zatrzymaliśmy obywatela Rosji, którego zadaniem było wykonanie egzekucji w Warszawie na obywatelu amerykańskim i ukraińskim równocześnie. Dzięki akcji ABW i Policji udało się temu zapobiec. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Though the prime minister said he was not allowed to name either the suspect or the target, he revealed that the latter was someone who is “inconvenient for Putin’s regime”. Tusk also gave no details of how the assassination was supposed to have been carried out, but said that it was foiled “at the last minute”. In a subsequent statement, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland’s security services, confirmed Tusk’s announcement and noted that the operation to prevent the attack had taken place in cooperation with the US. Police headquarters in Warsaw later revealed that the 29-year-old suspect had been charged with planning a murder and accepting an order to carry out murder in return for material or personal benefit. Both crimes carry jail terms of between two and 15 years. He has also been placed in court-approved pretrial detention. 7 sierpnia br. World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.
