World.title: Key players interviewed by Swans as club suspensions loom
World.content:
Key Sydney AFL players were quizzed individually by Swans officials on Tuesday as they face club-imposed suspensions of multiple matches over their conduct in Melbourne. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon confirmed the players could also face AFL sanctions irrespective of the outcome of a police investigation into a sexual assault allegation. Loading The five players, who had remained in Melbourne on Monday behind the rest of the team as it travelled back to Sydney, attended separate meetings with senior club and team officials away from Swans headquarters after driving home to NSW. The meetings were to discuss the events of Sunday night and Monday morning, which led to a police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. The investigation is being handled by Victoria Police’s sexual crimes squad.



“The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning,” Dillon said in a statement. “The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected,” he said. “Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light.” This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon and Chad Warner after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning.



This masthead is not suggesting any of the players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with inquiries. This masthead also contacted a representative of Swan Nick Blakey, who denied Blakey was involved in the incident. But the representative confirmed Blakey had also remained in Melbourne with his four teammates. Clockwise from left: Swans players Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard Earlier on Tuesday, two senior competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the players would be dealt with under the AFL rule that covers bringing the game into disrepute and conduct unbecoming. However, late on Tuesday the league said that rule would not immediately be applied.



Instead, the Swans, who are deeply unhappy with the behaviour of the players regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, will handle immediate penalties for the players. The players had been out drinking after Sunday night’s win over Essendon and returned to the team hotel in the early hours of Monday. The AFL has the power to suspend them under rule 2.3A, which prohibits conduct unbecoming or likely to prejudice the interests or reputation of the league. Any immediate club or league action would be separate to the Victoria Police investigation. A source close to the group of Swans players, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the players had been fully co-operative with the police probe.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation They said all five had been prepared to speak with police on Monday, but only one was ultimately quizzed. Police told the group they were not ready to conduct a formal interview or speak with any of the players acting as witnesses. The source said leading Melbourne criminal lawyer Tony Hargreaves was called in to assist the group before they were told they were free to leave and return to Sydney. Sydney is expected to make an announcement in response to the alleged incident, according to the competition sources, but that may not happen until Wednesday.



No player has been arrested and the AFL’s disciplinary action does not make any finding in relation to the allegation that remains under investigation by police. Instead, the AFL and the club have been examining the conduct of the players before and around the alleged incident, and whether their behaviour fell sufficiently below the standards expected of AFL footballers to warrant sanction under the league’s broad disrepute provisions. One of the most recent examples of an AFL suspension under this rule was for then Bulldog Bailey Smith, who was found guilty of conduct unbecoming and suspended for two matches in 2022. Smith admitted to using an illicit substance late in 2021. This masthead contacted all 36 of the Swans’ corporate partners. None were willing to comment on the incident, and so far, there is no indication any of the club’s sponsors will be walking away.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans However, a spokesperson for Origin expressed disappointment. “The club informed us about this incident yesterday, and we are incredibly disappointed. While the matter is subject to an investigation, it is not appropriate for us to comment any further,” the spokesperson said. The Swans players are now facing the prospect of missing not only Sydney’s final home-and-away match against North Melbourne on Sunday, but at least part of the Swans’ finals campaign. Sydney have already secured second position on the ladder and a home qualifying final. Any multi-game suspension would carry significant consequences for the club’s premiership aspirations. The Swans were forced to remain in Melbourne on Sunday night because Sydney Airport’s curfew prevented the team from returning home following its convincing win over Essendon at the MCG.



Several players subsequently went out drinking before returning to the Pullman, where the team and its staff were staying. Police attended the hotel on Monday after receiving the report of an alleged sexual assault.

World.title: Towers up to 30 storeys could be allowed near major shopping centre
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Towers up to 30 storeys could be allowed near major shopping centre William Davis August 18, 2026 — 7:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Towers up to 30 storeys could be allowed in some parts of Upper Mount Gravatt, with residents set to have their say on the proposal to transform their suburb. Under the precinct plan, taller buildings would likely be allowed to the north of the Garden City Shopping Centre, in the area running along Logan Road and Mount Gravatt Capalaba Road. It’s part of the contentious “tall-not-sprawl” push by the Schrinner LNP administration to increase housing supply in multiple suburbs that are well connected to existing infrastructure and public transport. The Upper Mount Gravatt address is a short walk to several major business hubs, including the shopping strip along Logan Road and Westfield Mount Gravatt. William Davis Details for Upper Mount Gravatt are yet to be determined, but building heights between five and 30 storeys are being considered for some areas.



The tallest buildings would likely be restricted to a small area close to shopping and other amenities. Brisbane City Council could also build shaded boulevards along Logan, Kessels and Mount Gravatt Capalaba roads, as well as new arcades. In Wynnum and Stones Corner, where precinct plans have already been established, buildings up to 15 and 20 storeys are allowed in some areas. These attracted fierce pushback from some sections of the community, who said the influx of new residents could overwhelm existing infrastructure and change the nature of their suburbs.



“We know that the key in responding to the housing shortage is to make sure there are options available for people’s needs at different times of their lives,” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said on Tuesday at City Hall. He said his administration’s policies would make it easier for new homeowners to get into the Brisbane market. Related Article City council NIMBYism or valid fears? The 15-storey plan that has this bayside community seeing red New zoning changes just down the road in Mount Gravatt will be adopted into the City Plan on September 18, as will changes to low-medium density residential zones across the city. The Labor opposition, which voted against the precinct plan in Wynnum, argued the changes brought to council on Tuesday represented a flawed strategy that prioritised supply above all other considerations.



“I reject the idea that this debate is simply between people who support more housing and people who oppose it,” Labor councillor Lucy Collier said. “The question isn’t about whether Brisbane grows, it’s how we grow, who that growth is for, and whether the infrastructure and services our community rely on grow with it.” Public consultation for the Upper Mount Gravatt precinct plan is due to open on August 21. World.title: How to talk to teenage boys about sex, according to experts
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsParenting How to talk to teenage boys about sex, according to experts Kimberly Gillan August 18, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

No sooner does it feel like our sons are starting to grasp their times tables than experts say it’s time to start weaving consent, sex and pornography into household conversations. With eSafety Commissioner research showing four in 10 surveyed adolescents first encountered pornography before they turned 13, there’s a good chance our boys are seeing explicit content far earlier than we realise, and developmental paediatrician Dr Billy Garvey says it could be giving them a dangerous idea of sex and consent. “A lot of parents don’t realise just how vulnerable kids are to pornography being the educator,” says Garvey, founder of Guiding Growing Minds and author of Ten Things I Wish You Knew About Raising Boys. Experts suggest having age-appropriate conversations with boys as young as nine. iStock “If we don’t talk about it and leave [sex education] to pornography, then there is a risk that violence within sex is normalised and role modelled, then their beliefs and behaviours are influenced completely external of us, often without our knowledge.”





“A lot of our parents sat us down before we went to a party and talked about drugs and alcohol and safe sex [but] this idea that one conversation will give them the skills to navigate it is just ridiculous,” Garvey says. “We know most kids see pornography three years before their first sexual experience, and 50 per cent of boys [see it] without seeking it out. It can be a very traumatic experience for these kids, especially if there is taboo talking about it. Then they sit in isolation with that experience, and it influences their beliefs, their expectations and how they feel about it; it normalises that stuff.” It might take a few false starts to get these open conversations flowing but Ben Vasiliou, chief executive of The Man Cave and author of the forthcoming book Better Man: Reclaiming Masculinity For Good, urges parents to keep trying. “I have a 16-year-old daughter and a 20-year-old son, and I’ve had many a conversation with my kids that just didn’t land,” he says. “But instead of being frustrated or just avoiding it, which I can understand, I just keep showing up and trying, chipping away.” Healthy role models are vital



Some good news for parents wanting to raise respectful men: you have more power than the manosphere. “The research says that young people are more inclined to listen to the role models and adults in their life than online influences,” Vasilou says. “Don’t feel like you’ve lost your kids to the digital world – you are still important, you are still respected, and you still have a role to play.” Garvey agrees that positive real-life relationships can be incredibly protective. “If you have healthy role models in the home, you can play the most violent video games and not become violent … and it’s the same with violent pornography,” Garvey says. “It’s the protective relationships that sit around these kids that [lead to] really healthy versions of masculinity. But if you have violence in the home, that’s when you’re at risk.”



Parents have more influence over their teenage children than they may assume. iStock If you can share some of your own memories of navigating sex, relationships and friendships as a young person, Garvey says you’ll help set your son up for success. “Self-disclosure is really important. A lot of parents are nervous about saying what they were really like, but it’s really important for boys to hear our stories of anger, insecurity, fear, rejection and jealousy,” he says. “A boy might go, ‘My mates are saying they’re having sex with people’ or ‘Do I be derogatory to women to prove myself?’ and a dad who can say, ‘This is what it was like for me when I was 14, I remember the pressure and I learnt that a healthier version would be this’ … that’s really powerful.” Accountability with care



Garvey says most teenagers and men who engage in antisocial behaviour and violent acts “shot up hundreds of flares” throughout their childhood and adolescence to show they were struggling and needed more help. Related Article Parenting Celebrities are shrinking. Here’s how to talk to your children “Violence erupts out of them because of insecurities and fears and anxieties and rejection and all that stuff that they haven’t learned how to handle well,” he says. Vasilou says today’s parents have a responsibility to ensure their sons have a deep understanding of consent. “Teaching consent is about enthusiastic participation – if someone is silent, frozen, intoxicated, frightened or resisting, that is not a green light; it’s a red flag,” he says.



“The goal is to raise boys who can recognise another person’s humanity, can read boundaries, can handle rejection and ultimately can intervene when their mates cross the line.” If you’re flabbergasted by something your son has said or done, starting with questions can be a good way to learn about the motivation behind his behaviour –and the peer pressure or culture he might be up against – then enforce accountability. Vasilou says open-ended questions can help parents understand where their children are coming from, which can then help them enquire further and dig deep. “We can’t just accept accountability as an apology after the fact – we need explicit accountability, which means we can’t be euphemising harmful behaviour, laughing it off or calling it banter because we are seeing those things leading to pretty harmful [outcomes],” he says. “Accountability involves recognising the harm and consequences, changing behaviour and where appropriate, repair [of] that particular situation.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: Ralph Carr vows to fight for his freedom as lawyer rebuked over ‘emotional’ speech
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Ralph Carr vows to fight for his freedom as lawyer rebuked over ‘emotional’ speech Erin Pearson August 18, 2026 — 6:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sports and entertainment manager Ralph Carr plans to fight for his freedom for as long as it takes, a court has heard as his lawyer branded Carr’s rape conviction the most obvious miscarriage of justice he had seen in a decades-long career. But Dermot Dann’s strong defence of his client was met by tense debate from the judge and from the prosecutor, who accused the King’s Counsel of making inappropriate political and emotional statements. A court sketch of Ralph Carr. Paul Tyquin The second day of Carr’s pre-sentence hearing was underscored by both sides trading legal blows amid looks of frustration, eye rolling and whispering throughout hours of legal argument over his application to stay the case pending an appeal. Carr, who once counted Brownlow medallist Dustin Martin as a client and business partner and was married to singer Tina Arena, was found guilty last month of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault, following a jury trial in the County Court. He maintains his innocence.



On Tuesday, lawyers for the 66-year-old argued there had been a serious miscarriage of justice and the jury verdict was unsafe. Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted Dann acknowledged his application to stay the case was a rare legal move only to be used in the most exceptional circumstances. “We submit that anyone who was in this court … and saw and heard the complainant give evidence in this trial should be very, very concerned and very, very uncomfortable about the guilty verdicts,” he said. “There should be no one who feels comfortable with those verdicts, and anyone who does ... has lost sight of what justice is and justice means.”



Dann said that in his 35 years of experience, Carr’s case was the most obvious miscarriage of justice he had seen. But Judge Frank Gucciardo told Dann his client would not be the first convicted man to claim his innocence and that it was inappropriate to overstate claims and express personal views at that point of the hearing. “I respectfully differ,” Dann replied. Gucciardo said he was not troubled by the jury verdicts and would not reassess the evidence. He said the jurors were conscientious, engaged by the evidence and cross-examination, and took copious notes before days of deliberations. “The whole process seemed to be exactly how it should’ve been. It seems to me you’ve got the hurdle to jump,” the trial judge said.



In carving out the issues for the defence, Dann said the complainant’s evidence changed during her six days in the witness box compared with what she had previously told police. Dustin Martin poses with Carr, then the footballer’s manager, after winning the 2017 Brownlow Medal. Getty Images Differences, he said, included the length of the alleged rapes and whether Carr was clothed or partially undressed. Dann also maintained the complainant had a financial motive to lie, pointing to a pending civil case. A future appeal, he said, had good prospects, and he pointed to his client’s declining mental health and placement in solitary confinement as reasons for his possible release on bail if the stay application was granted. Prosecutor Matthew Fisher said he had serious concerns about how Dann was referring to Carr’s plight and any potential miscarriage of justice.



“We are very concerned on this side of the Bar table. To make a political or emotional speech to your honour … is entirely inappropriate,” Fisher said. Related Article Courts ‘Like a living hell’: Rapist Ralph Carr unrecognisable in court appearance “We hope he hasn’t made that statement to your honour to garner or attract some sort of media attention to his client’s cause. It was open to the jury to reach the verdicts that they did.” The court heard the woman had elected not to read or compile a victim impact statement for the court. Her evidence during the trial was held in closed court. Carr was found guilty in July after the jury heard he and the victim had been consuming alcohol and cocaine at his home in 2023 when he raped her.



His identity was suppressed for three years after his legal team obtained a suppression order to conceal his alleged involvement in the assault citing mental health concerns. On Monday, the court heard Carr was confined to his prison cell for 23 hours a day, and believes the verdict has destroyed his career. Dann said his client’s declining mental health warranted mitigation of his sentencing along with Carr’s lack of criminal history, prior good character, and the significant contribution he had made to the community. The pre-sentence hearing and stay application will continue on Wednesday. World.title: Minister denies eye roll at veterans pleading for healthcare funding
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Minister denies eye roll at veterans pleading for healthcare funding Brittany Busch August 18, 2026 — 6:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Veterans’ Affairs Minister Matt Keogh has conceded he made a mistake by refusing to meet former defence personnel who are calling for Labor to scrap a cap on allied health service funding, but denied accusations he rolled his eyes at the veterans and refused to shake their hands. The Coalition of Veterans’ Voices is in Canberra this week urging the government to abandon an annual $5000 cap on allied health services for veterans, introduced in the May budget and set to start next year. Minister for Veterans’ Affairs Matt Keogh during question time on Tuesday. Dominic Lorrimer Keogh met the advocacy group on Monday after the Coalition launched a scathing attack on the minister. The allied health services cap has further strained the minister’s relationship with the veteran community after he abandoned plans to scrap funding for the Invictus Games and pull travel assistance funding for the parents of Victoria Cross recipient Cameron Baird. Former pilot Dr Tim Nelson said he had no faith in the department’s ability to administer the cap and accused Keogh of rolling his eyes during Monday’s meeting.



Related Article City life The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story “It was obvious he did not want to be there,” Nelson told a press conference in Canberra on Tuesday. “He walked into the room, refused to shake our hand, sat down with his arms crossed, and rolled his eyes.” Former navy clearance diver John Armfield, whose brother died by suicide, said Keogh was too focused on the budget bottom line. “Minister Keogh forgets he was elected to serve, not self-serve,” Armfield said. “The budget’s obviously playing a role here. He wants the savings to go with that.” Labor identified the $6.6 billion veterans fund as a target for savings in May, and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher likened it to the NDIS because dodgy doctors were skimming payments meant for retired defence personnel. The budget measures aim to claw back more than $700 million over four years.



Veterans with critical needs can apply for greater funding for services, including occupational therapists, physiotherapists and psychologists, once they reach the cap, which Labor says is necessary to prevent overcharging. But veterans have argued that it creates an extra hurdle for those in crisis. Keogh said on Tuesday he had made a mistake for not agreeing to meet the veterans in the first instance, but rejected Nelson’s characterisation of his behaviour in the meeting. “I acknowledge that I got it wrong not agreeing to meet with them last week when that initial request came,” he said. “When I came into that room, I met with them, and they were sitting down. I said, ‘Relax, and I want to hear what you want to tell me’ … and I shook the hands of those people who attended that meeting as we finished that meeting, to be clear.” Keogh acknowledged the distrust of the department within the veteran community, and said a discussion paper to consult on the changes would be released soon.



He has argued Labor is making it easier for veterans to access allied health services by committing nearly $170 million to increasing fees for providers that had been threatening to cut back services, and said the government was striving to ensure veterans did not pay a gap fee. Opposition defence industry and personnel spokesman Phillip Thompson, himself a veteran, said the community Keogh represented had lost faith in his leadership. Thompson has attacked Keogh over the “cruel cuts”, referencing his own mental health struggles and warning that veterans were planning to take their own lives when they hit the annual cap because they swore to never be a burden on their families. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said allied health services saved lives, and called on the prime minister to meet those affected by the cap. “Those that do sacrifice for our nation don’t just leave scars on the battlefield. They are left with scars for life, and understandably, they need help … and support from professionals,” he said.

World.title: Labor’s controversial gambling bill will pass – with fresh headaches for the government
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalGambling Labor’s controversial gambling bill will pass – with fresh headaches for the government Natassia Chrysanthos and Paul Sakkal Updated August 18, 2026 — 6:23pm ,first published 2:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians who don’t want to see gambling ads online will be able to opt out with a new “AdStop” regime but the government will be scrambling to design a workable scheme and deal with privacy concerns as its wagering laws become mired in complexity. Last-minute amendments will not block freebies for punters as former addicts and their families had hoped. A new rule stopping inducements for problem gamblers still needs a definition of high-risk customers to give it teeth, setting up a fresh fight with the gambling industry. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese puts the Gambling Reform Bill 2026 to the House of Representatives as Communications Minister Anika Wells looks on. Dominic Lorrimer The amendments were introduced on Tuesday in a compromise deal between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor. The opposition leader also signed off on Labor’s National Disability Insurance Scheme overhaul, which was due to pass the Senate on Tuesday night, in exchange for the government expediting moves to rid a “widow’s tax” from tax changes. Labor was forced to amend its gambling legislation after a Senate inquiry into the laws this month heard alarming testimony about addicts, including former NRL player Luke Bateman, being lured into wagering with drugs, escorts and thousands of dollars in free bets.



More than three years after the late Labor MP Peta Murphy’s bipartisan report recommended a total ban on gambling ads and inducements, the Labor caucus signed off on the changes. Albanese told MPs the government had struck a balance between protecting children and permitting Australia’s betting culture, and told parliament that the revised package was “the most significant gambling advertising reform by any Australian government ever”. Loading Some Labor MPs said the changes were a good start and could be strengthened over time, but several were downhearted. Others said the government’s late changes made the package so complex as to be unworkable. In a sign of discontent about the final bill and the fractious process leading up to it, some Liberal MPs yelled complaints in question time as the prime minister talked up the reform. Cook MP Simon Kennedy heckled Albanese about having been embarrassed into strengthening the bill.



All the independent crossbenchers, many of whom have campaigned for stronger gambling action, voted against the bill when it came to the House of Representatives on Tuesday night. “Only three hours of debate after three long years of waiting,” said Curtin MP Kate Chaney. “Trust in politics is eroded when the major parties do deals like this on legislation that are made for political convenience, not based on evidence.” They were joined by the Greens, Nationals MP Pat Conaghan and Liberal MP Andrew Wallace, who crossed the floor against Coalition policy for the first time in his 10-year parliamentary career, saying the amendments “don’t go anywhere near” fixing problem gambling. “I can’t in good conscience vote for [the bill],” Wallace said. Under the original package announced in April, viewers will see no more than three gambling ads per hour on television. There will also be a phased-in ad ban for stadiums and jerseys, a ban on sports stars promoting wagering, and tighter limits on radio ads in school pick-up hours. Online platforms will have to offer registered adult users the option of opting out of digital ads.



A further amendment applies the same hourly ad limit to television and online streaming services, after the Coalition pushed Labor to reverse its plans to give streaming services carte blanche if registered users didn’t opt out of watching gambling ads. Viewers won’t see gambling ads for 15 minutes before a game – an extension from the previously planned five minutes – and hourly ad limit will start an hour earlier, at 5am. The laws will have to be reviewed in three years and betting companies will be levied to pay for compliance of the online advertising opt-out regime. Betting inducements Opposition communication spokeswoman Sarah Henderson said the Coalition was “very pleased to have prosecuted these amendments in the best interests of all Australians”.



“We heard some damning evidence, including from the likes of Mr Bateman, so this, for the first time, combats predatory inducements,” she said. But the new rules for betting inducements – which include free bonus bets and the services of VIP agents – dismayed advocates who wanted an all-out ban, recommended by the Murphy report. Related Article Gambling ‘I can’t stop to save my own life’: Parents read son’s final plea on gambling addiction In addition to banning inducements for risky gamblers, gambling companies will have to wait 14 days after someone opens an account to offer them any promotions. There will be a 90-day wait time for people attempting to move off the self-exclusion platform BetStop. Reform advocates argue the industry cannot be trusted, given evidence to the Senate inquiry about problem gamblers lured with free bets. One person was offered $50,000 in free bets despite losing about $500,000 in a month.



The government will move to define high-risk gamblers in law, sources said. But the threshold has not been determined. It could gauge someone’s betting frequency, for example, or how much money had been drained from their bank account. Given promotions represent about 30 per cent of turnover for the racing industry, this will set up a fresh fight between the government and gambling sector, which will push officials to adopt existing thresholds already used in some states and territories. Independent MP Allegra Spender said either way the law would not intervene until people had already become problem gamblers. “We are literally providing the pathway ... for people’s lives to be ruined by gambling, and then say: ‘Oh, by the time that you get there, we’ll see if we can do anything to make this a little bit easier for you’,” she said. “The government has an option. The opposition has an option. It could just go out there and ban inducements altogether ... It is deeply disappointing to all the people who came and gave their time and effort to all the inquiries.



“Because we could be making Australians safer right now, and we have chosen not to, and that is a decision that has been made by the major parties.” Advertising opt-out The other amendment that will create a technical headache for the government is the opt-out regime. This was another push from the Coalition, concerned that people would be reluctant to opt out of advertising across all their online accounts. The “AdStop” scheme will be administered by the Australian Communications and Media Authority, using funding from a levy to be imposed on gambling companies.



Government sources said it could involve people nominating either their email address or mobile phone number to the ACMA register. Online platforms would then have to reconcile their customer details with the register and would not be allowed to show gambling ads to registered accounts. This would apply to online streaming services as well as social media accounts. But the register won’t be ready when the new advertising rules come into force on January 1, given it will require time to work out and likely raise privacy concerns. The peak body representing firms such as Sportsbet, Responsible Wagering Australia, said the AdStop proposal was unwieldy. “Betstop, which is a simpler concept, took more than four years from inception to implementation,” the outfit’s chief executive, Kai Cantwell, said.

World.title: ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies Nick McKenzie August 18, 2026 — 7:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leading Australian infrastructure firm working on major state and federally backed projects has been implicated in a suspected plot that allegedly saw a crew of Melbourne bikie enforcers travel to Brisbane to threaten to burn down the house and kill the children of a CFMEU activist. A blow-by-blow account of the alleged stand-over plot was unveiled during the grilling of an executive from construction giant BMD at the Queensland’s Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and building industry misconduct. But rather than the focus being on the misdeeds of the construction union, the commission heard that BMD’s security firm had recruited three feared Melbourne Comanchero identities to confront a CFMEU activist as he worked his crane shift on the Albanese and Queensland government-funded $350 million Centenary Bridge project in June 2024. The revelations at the Queensland inquiry give Australians a taste of what is likely to be unveiled at the promised and upcoming Victorian royal commission. Half of the key subjects at Tuesday’s hearing in Brisbane were from Melbourne and are variously entrenched in both Victoria’s underworld and its building sector.



The hearing has also placed immense scrutiny on BMD, which is currently working Victoria’s Eastern Freeway Upgrade, the new Western Sydney International Airport and Queensland’s Rockhampton Ring Road. Asked about the evidence heard at the commission suggesting BMD associated with underworld-linked figures in the alleged Centenary Bridge stand-over incident and whether BMD’s internal investigations into the matter was adequate, the company’s spokesperson said: “BMD has additional representatives to appear over the coming days and it would be premature for us to comment.” Bemir Saracevic. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU On Tuesday afternoon, the commission heard crane driver Cody Raymond had alleged in a statement that during the 2024 altercation, the now former Melbourne-based president of the Comancheros, Bemir Saracevic, introduced himself as “Benji from the Comos” and said he represented BMD’s security firm, Host. The statement claimed Saracevic threatened extreme violence after Raymond allegedly argued days earlier with Host’s owner, Melbourne businessman Gary Samuel. Raymond had been suspected by Samuel of leaking information about the BMD project to the CFMEU, the commission heard.



Months before the stand-over, BMD hired Samuel and his company Host to counter the CFMEU’s increasingly aggressive tactics on the bridge project. Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Not to be messed with’: Criminals recruited for country’s biggest wind farm The union ultimately wanted to force BMD, which is aligned to the rival Australian Workers Union, to bow to CFMEU demands. Raymond, an active CFMEU member, said in his statement that, as Samuel watched on, Saracevic, backed by two Comanchero gang affiliates, told him he would “f---ing burn your house down c--- and kill your kids”. Saracevic also allegedly told Raymond that “I know where you live” and, in audio captured on CCTV of the incident, warned that he should not contact the police.



The two other bikie-linked men with Saracevic were Mark Ahern, a former treasurer of the Comancheros who was jailed for torching a Melbourne strip club in 2016, and Kristomir Bjelogrlic, a senior gang associate with extensive interests in Victoria’s construction industry. BMD executive Robert Pickard repeatedly denied knowing about the presence or actions of the Melbourne Comanchero trio under a grilling from counsel assisting Eddy Gisonda. Rob Pickard (right), General Manager, Queensland and Northern Territory, BMD Constructions is seen being questioned by Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC (left) during the Commission of Inquiry. AAPIMAGE The evidence, including phone records and CCTV, showed that Pickard and a fellow BMD executive, human resources chief Steve Thomas, were in frequent phone contact with Samuel as he ferried the Comancheros from Brisbane airport to confront Raymond. CCTV also showed Pickard and Thomas emerging from a carpark moments before the bikie trio and Samuel also appeared to walk from the same carpark.



Pickard and Thomas also appeared on the CCTV to be leading, at a distance of about 80 metres, the Comanchero figures and Samuel as they approached the Centenary Bridge project where Raymond was operating his crane. Kris Bjelogrlic. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU When the four men initially confronted him, Raymond said he “felt like they were ready to roll on gang bash me”. Pickard strongly denied that he was working with or knew anything about the bikie-linked trio or their confrontation of Raymond until the crane driver complained about the alleged stand-over shortly after it occurred and Pickard ordered an investigation. Gisonda told Commissioner Stuart Wood, KC, that there was no evidence that Pickard or Thomas had communicated directly with the Comanchero trio, instead saying the “common link” between the gang affiliated men and BMD was Samuel.



During his questioning on Tuesday, Pickard denied Raymond’s statement that he had volunteered to help “squash” the fall-out from the Centenary Bridge incident by leveraging BMD’s influence over Host as its security sub-contractor. Pickard also said he had no recollection of saying that he knew Host was linked to the Comancheros, while the CFMEU was linked to the Bandidos. Instead, the senior BMD executive told the commission he offered Raymond his sympathy for being on the receiving end of threats, saying that it was “unacceptable for any wife or other family members to be feeling that way, including himself [Raymond]” . With the questioning of Pickard set to continue on Wednesday, BMD is now embroiled in a potentially growing scandal given that the evidence led by Gisonda places the infrastructure giant in close proximity to an alleged underworld stand-over on a taxpayer-backed site. BMD’s hiring of Samuel also raises major questions for the firm. In June last year, an investigation by this masthead demonstrated that basic due diligence would have revealed Samuel’s repeated business dealings with Melbourne’s underworld.



For instance, historical records available online from Victoria’s Lawyer X Royal Commission show that, in 2011, Samuel advised a building firm owned by Mick Gatto and his fellow underworld identity Mat Tomas. Tomas and Gatto both achieved notoriety in the 2000s by beating gangland murder charges, and, by separately forging deep ties to former CFMEU boss John Setka. Samuel later went into a failed business venture with Tomas and also ran the Victorian operations of the now-deceased labour hire king Kevin McHugh, whom federal police charged in 2020 with money laundering offences and tax fraud and who was also an associate of corrupt NSW CFMEU boss Darren Greenfield. Samuel declined to answer specific questions when quizzed by this masthead last year, but said in a statement at the time that it was “important to acknowledge the ongoing rivalry between the CFMEU and the AWU” and that “certain factions of the CFMEU have been linked to organised crime”. “Our company is law-abiding and has no link to organised crime,” he said. World.title: Key players interviewed by Swans as club suspensions loom
World.content:
Key Sydney AFL players were quizzed individually by Swans officials on Tuesday as they face club-imposed suspensions of multiple matches over their conduct in Melbourne. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon confirmed the players could also face AFL sanctions irrespective of the outcome of a police investigation into a sexual assault allegation. Loading The five players, who had remained in Melbourne on Monday behind the rest of the team as it travelled back to Sydney, attended separate meetings with senior club and team officials away from Swans headquarters after driving home to NSW. The meetings were to discuss the events of Sunday night and Monday morning, which led to a police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. The investigation is being handled by Victoria Police’s sexual crimes squad.



“The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning,” Dillon said in a statement. “The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected,” he said. “Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light.” This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon and Chad Warner after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning.



This masthead is not suggesting any of the players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with inquiries. This masthead also contacted a representative of Swan Nick Blakey, who denied Blakey was involved in the incident. But the representative confirmed Blakey had also remained in Melbourne with his four teammates. Clockwise from left: Swans players Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard Earlier on Tuesday, two senior competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the players would be dealt with under the AFL rule that covers bringing the game into disrepute and conduct unbecoming. However, late on Tuesday the league said that rule would not immediately be applied.



Instead, the Swans, who are deeply unhappy with the behaviour of the players regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, will handle immediate penalties for the players. The players had been out drinking after Sunday night’s win over Essendon and returned to the team hotel in the early hours of Monday. The AFL has the power to suspend them under rule 2.3A, which prohibits conduct unbecoming or likely to prejudice the interests or reputation of the league. Any immediate club or league action would be separate to the Victoria Police investigation. A source close to the group of Swans players, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the players had been fully co-operative with the police probe.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation They said all five had been prepared to speak with police on Monday, but only one was ultimately quizzed. Police told the group they were not ready to conduct a formal interview or speak with any of the players acting as witnesses. The source said leading Melbourne criminal lawyer Tony Hargreaves was called in to assist the group before they were told they were free to leave and return to Sydney. Sydney is expected to make an announcement in response to the alleged incident, according to the competition sources, but that may not happen until Wednesday.



No player has been arrested and the AFL’s disciplinary action does not make any finding in relation to the allegation that remains under investigation by police. Instead, the AFL and the club have been examining the conduct of the players before and around the alleged incident, and whether their behaviour fell sufficiently below the standards expected of AFL footballers to warrant sanction under the league’s broad disrepute provisions. One of the most recent examples of an AFL suspension under this rule was for then Bulldog Bailey Smith, who was found guilty of conduct unbecoming and suspended for two matches in 2022. Smith admitted to using an illicit substance late in 2021. This masthead contacted all 36 of the Swans’ corporate partners. None were willing to comment on the incident, and so far, there is no indication any of the club’s sponsors will be walking away.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans However, a spokesperson for Origin expressed disappointment. “The club informed us about this incident yesterday, and we are incredibly disappointed. While the matter is subject to an investigation, it is not appropriate for us to comment any further,” the spokesperson said. The Swans players are now facing the prospect of missing not only Sydney’s final home-and-away match against North Melbourne on Sunday, but at least part of the Swans’ finals campaign. Sydney have already secured second position on the ladder and a home qualifying final. Any multi-game suspension would carry significant consequences for the club’s premiership aspirations. The Swans were forced to remain in Melbourne on Sunday night because Sydney Airport’s curfew prevented the team from returning home following its convincing win over Essendon at the MCG.



Several players subsequently went out drinking before returning to the Pullman, where the team and its staff were staying. Police attended the hotel on Monday after receiving the report of an alleged sexual assault.

World.title: Towers up to 30 storeys could be allowed near major shopping centre
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Towers up to 30 storeys could be allowed near major shopping centre William Davis August 18, 2026 — 7:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Towers up to 30 storeys could be allowed in some parts of Upper Mount Gravatt, with residents set to have their say on the proposal to transform their suburb. Under the precinct plan, taller buildings would likely be allowed to the north of the Garden City Shopping Centre, in the area running along Logan Road and Mount Gravatt Capalaba Road. It’s part of the contentious “tall-not-sprawl” push by the Schrinner LNP administration to increase housing supply in multiple suburbs that are well connected to existing infrastructure and public transport. The Upper Mount Gravatt address is a short walk to several major business hubs, including the shopping strip along Logan Road and Westfield Mount Gravatt. William Davis Details for Upper Mount Gravatt are yet to be determined, but building heights between five and 30 storeys are being considered for some areas.



The tallest buildings would likely be restricted to a small area close to shopping and other amenities. Brisbane City Council could also build shaded boulevards along Logan, Kessels and Mount Gravatt Capalaba roads, as well as new arcades. In Wynnum and Stones Corner, where precinct plans have already been established, buildings up to 15 and 20 storeys are allowed in some areas. These attracted fierce pushback from some sections of the community, who said the influx of new residents could overwhelm existing infrastructure and change the nature of their suburbs.



“We know that the key in responding to the housing shortage is to make sure there are options available for people’s needs at different times of their lives,” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said on Tuesday at City Hall. He said his administration’s policies would make it easier for new homeowners to get into the Brisbane market. Related Article City council NIMBYism or valid fears? The 15-storey plan that has this bayside community seeing red New zoning changes just down the road in Mount Gravatt will be adopted into the City Plan on September 18, as will changes to low-medium density residential zones across the city. The Labor opposition, which voted against the precinct plan in Wynnum, argued the changes brought to council on Tuesday represented a flawed strategy that prioritised supply above all other considerations.



“I reject the idea that this debate is simply between people who support more housing and people who oppose it,” Labor councillor Lucy Collier said. “The question isn’t about whether Brisbane grows, it’s how we grow, who that growth is for, and whether the infrastructure and services our community rely on grow with it.” Public consultation for the Upper Mount Gravatt precinct plan is due to open on August 21. World.title: How to talk to teenage boys about sex, according to experts
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsParenting How to talk to teenage boys about sex, according to experts Kimberly Gillan August 18, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

No sooner does it feel like our sons are starting to grasp their times tables than experts say it’s time to start weaving consent, sex and pornography into household conversations. With eSafety Commissioner research showing four in 10 surveyed adolescents first encountered pornography before they turned 13, there’s a good chance our boys are seeing explicit content far earlier than we realise, and developmental paediatrician Dr Billy Garvey says it could be giving them a dangerous idea of sex and consent. “A lot of parents don’t realise just how vulnerable kids are to pornography being the educator,” says Garvey, founder of Guiding Growing Minds and author of Ten Things I Wish You Knew About Raising Boys. Experts suggest having age-appropriate conversations with boys as young as nine. iStock “If we don’t talk about it and leave [sex education] to pornography, then there is a risk that violence within sex is normalised and role modelled, then their beliefs and behaviours are influenced completely external of us, often without our knowledge.”





“A lot of our parents sat us down before we went to a party and talked about drugs and alcohol and safe sex [but] this idea that one conversation will give them the skills to navigate it is just ridiculous,” Garvey says. “We know most kids see pornography three years before their first sexual experience, and 50 per cent of boys [see it] without seeking it out. It can be a very traumatic experience for these kids, especially if there is taboo talking about it. Then they sit in isolation with that experience, and it influences their beliefs, their expectations and how they feel about it; it normalises that stuff.” It might take a few false starts to get these open conversations flowing but Ben Vasiliou, chief executive of The Man Cave and author of the forthcoming book Better Man: Reclaiming Masculinity For Good, urges parents to keep trying. “I have a 16-year-old daughter and a 20-year-old son, and I’ve had many a conversation with my kids that just didn’t land,” he says. “But instead of being frustrated or just avoiding it, which I can understand, I just keep showing up and trying, chipping away.” Healthy role models are vital



Some good news for parents wanting to raise respectful men: you have more power than the manosphere. “The research says that young people are more inclined to listen to the role models and adults in their life than online influences,” Vasilou says. “Don’t feel like you’ve lost your kids to the digital world – you are still important, you are still respected, and you still have a role to play.” Garvey agrees that positive real-life relationships can be incredibly protective. “If you have healthy role models in the home, you can play the most violent video games and not become violent … and it’s the same with violent pornography,” Garvey says. “It’s the protective relationships that sit around these kids that [lead to] really healthy versions of masculinity. But if you have violence in the home, that’s when you’re at risk.”



Parents have more influence over their teenage children than they may assume. iStock If you can share some of your own memories of navigating sex, relationships and friendships as a young person, Garvey says you’ll help set your son up for success. “Self-disclosure is really important. A lot of parents are nervous about saying what they were really like, but it’s really important for boys to hear our stories of anger, insecurity, fear, rejection and jealousy,” he says. “A boy might go, ‘My mates are saying they’re having sex with people’ or ‘Do I be derogatory to women to prove myself?’ and a dad who can say, ‘This is what it was like for me when I was 14, I remember the pressure and I learnt that a healthier version would be this’ … that’s really powerful.” Accountability with care



Garvey says most teenagers and men who engage in antisocial behaviour and violent acts “shot up hundreds of flares” throughout their childhood and adolescence to show they were struggling and needed more help. Related Article Parenting Celebrities are shrinking. Here’s how to talk to your children “Violence erupts out of them because of insecurities and fears and anxieties and rejection and all that stuff that they haven’t learned how to handle well,” he says. Vasilou says today’s parents have a responsibility to ensure their sons have a deep understanding of consent. “Teaching consent is about enthusiastic participation – if someone is silent, frozen, intoxicated, frightened or resisting, that is not a green light; it’s a red flag,” he says.



“The goal is to raise boys who can recognise another person’s humanity, can read boundaries, can handle rejection and ultimately can intervene when their mates cross the line.” If you’re flabbergasted by something your son has said or done, starting with questions can be a good way to learn about the motivation behind his behaviour –and the peer pressure or culture he might be up against – then enforce accountability. Vasilou says open-ended questions can help parents understand where their children are coming from, which can then help them enquire further and dig deep. “We can’t just accept accountability as an apology after the fact – we need explicit accountability, which means we can’t be euphemising harmful behaviour, laughing it off or calling it banter because we are seeing those things leading to pretty harmful [outcomes],” he says. “Accountability involves recognising the harm and consequences, changing behaviour and where appropriate, repair [of] that particular situation.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Ralph Carr vows to fight for his freedom as lawyer rebuked over ‘emotional’ speech
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Ralph Carr vows to fight for his freedom as lawyer rebuked over ‘emotional’ speech Erin Pearson August 18, 2026 — 6:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sports and entertainment manager Ralph Carr plans to fight for his freedom for as long as it takes, a court has heard as his lawyer branded Carr’s rape conviction the most obvious miscarriage of justice he had seen in a decades-long career. But Dermot Dann’s strong defence of his client was met by tense debate from the judge and from the prosecutor, who accused the King’s Counsel of making inappropriate political and emotional statements. A court sketch of Ralph Carr. Paul Tyquin The second day of Carr’s pre-sentence hearing was underscored by both sides trading legal blows amid looks of frustration, eye rolling and whispering throughout hours of legal argument over his application to stay the case pending an appeal. Carr, who once counted Brownlow medallist Dustin Martin as a client and business partner and was married to singer Tina Arena, was found guilty last month of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault, following a jury trial in the County Court. He maintains his innocence.



On Tuesday, lawyers for the 66-year-old argued there had been a serious miscarriage of justice and the jury verdict was unsafe. Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted Dann acknowledged his application to stay the case was a rare legal move only to be used in the most exceptional circumstances. “We submit that anyone who was in this court … and saw and heard the complainant give evidence in this trial should be very, very concerned and very, very uncomfortable about the guilty verdicts,” he said. “There should be no one who feels comfortable with those verdicts, and anyone who does ... has lost sight of what justice is and justice means.”



Dann said that in his 35 years of experience, Carr’s case was the most obvious miscarriage of justice he had seen. But Judge Frank Gucciardo told Dann his client would not be the first convicted man to claim his innocence and that it was inappropriate to overstate claims and express personal views at that point of the hearing. “I respectfully differ,” Dann replied. Gucciardo said he was not troubled by the jury verdicts and would not reassess the evidence. He said the jurors were conscientious, engaged by the evidence and cross-examination, and took copious notes before days of deliberations. “The whole process seemed to be exactly how it should’ve been. It seems to me you’ve got the hurdle to jump,” the trial judge said.



In carving out the issues for the defence, Dann said the complainant’s evidence changed during her six days in the witness box compared with what she had previously told police. Dustin Martin poses with Carr, then the footballer’s manager, after winning the 2017 Brownlow Medal. Getty Images Differences, he said, included the length of the alleged rapes and whether Carr was clothed or partially undressed. Dann also maintained the complainant had a financial motive to lie, pointing to a pending civil case. A future appeal, he said, had good prospects, and he pointed to his client’s declining mental health and placement in solitary confinement as reasons for his possible release on bail if the stay application was granted. Prosecutor Matthew Fisher said he had serious concerns about how Dann was referring to Carr’s plight and any potential miscarriage of justice.



“We are very concerned on this side of the Bar table. To make a political or emotional speech to your honour … is entirely inappropriate,” Fisher said. Related Article Courts ‘Like a living hell’: Rapist Ralph Carr unrecognisable in court appearance “We hope he hasn’t made that statement to your honour to garner or attract some sort of media attention to his client’s cause. It was open to the jury to reach the verdicts that they did.” The court heard the woman had elected not to read or compile a victim impact statement for the court. Her evidence during the trial was held in closed court. Carr was found guilty in July after the jury heard he and the victim had been consuming alcohol and cocaine at his home in 2023 when he raped her.



His identity was suppressed for three years after his legal team obtained a suppression order to conceal his alleged involvement in the assault citing mental health concerns. On Monday, the court heard Carr was confined to his prison cell for 23 hours a day, and believes the verdict has destroyed his career. Dann said his client’s declining mental health warranted mitigation of his sentencing along with Carr’s lack of criminal history, prior good character, and the significant contribution he had made to the community. The pre-sentence hearing and stay application will continue on Wednesday. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: Minister denies eye roll at veterans pleading for healthcare funding
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Minister denies eye roll at veterans pleading for healthcare funding Brittany Busch August 18, 2026 — 6:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Veterans’ Affairs Minister Matt Keogh has conceded he made a mistake by refusing to meet former defence personnel who are calling for Labor to scrap a cap on allied health service funding, but denied accusations he rolled his eyes at the veterans and refused to shake their hands. The Coalition of Veterans’ Voices is in Canberra this week urging the government to abandon an annual $5000 cap on allied health services for veterans, introduced in the May budget and set to start next year. Minister for Veterans’ Affairs Matt Keogh during question time on Tuesday. Dominic Lorrimer Keogh met the advocacy group on Monday after the Coalition launched a scathing attack on the minister. The allied health services cap has further strained the minister’s relationship with the veteran community after he abandoned plans to scrap funding for the Invictus Games and pull travel assistance funding for the parents of Victoria Cross recipient Cameron Baird. Former pilot Dr Tim Nelson said he had no faith in the department’s ability to administer the cap and accused Keogh of rolling his eyes during Monday’s meeting.



Related Article City life The knock on the door: 57 years on, a Vietnam War widow tells her story “It was obvious he did not want to be there,” Nelson told a press conference in Canberra on Tuesday. “He walked into the room, refused to shake our hand, sat down with his arms crossed, and rolled his eyes.” Former navy clearance diver John Armfield, whose brother died by suicide, said Keogh was too focused on the budget bottom line. “Minister Keogh forgets he was elected to serve, not self-serve,” Armfield said. “The budget’s obviously playing a role here. He wants the savings to go with that.” Labor identified the $6.6 billion veterans fund as a target for savings in May, and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher likened it to the NDIS because dodgy doctors were skimming payments meant for retired defence personnel. The budget measures aim to claw back more than $700 million over four years.



Veterans with critical needs can apply for greater funding for services, including occupational therapists, physiotherapists and psychologists, once they reach the cap, which Labor says is necessary to prevent overcharging. But veterans have argued that it creates an extra hurdle for those in crisis. Keogh said on Tuesday he had made a mistake for not agreeing to meet the veterans in the first instance, but rejected Nelson’s characterisation of his behaviour in the meeting. “I acknowledge that I got it wrong not agreeing to meet with them last week when that initial request came,” he said. “When I came into that room, I met with them, and they were sitting down. I said, ‘Relax, and I want to hear what you want to tell me’ … and I shook the hands of those people who attended that meeting as we finished that meeting, to be clear.” Keogh acknowledged the distrust of the department within the veteran community, and said a discussion paper to consult on the changes would be released soon.



He has argued Labor is making it easier for veterans to access allied health services by committing nearly $170 million to increasing fees for providers that had been threatening to cut back services, and said the government was striving to ensure veterans did not pay a gap fee. Opposition defence industry and personnel spokesman Phillip Thompson, himself a veteran, said the community Keogh represented had lost faith in his leadership. Thompson has attacked Keogh over the “cruel cuts”, referencing his own mental health struggles and warning that veterans were planning to take their own lives when they hit the annual cap because they swore to never be a burden on their families. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said allied health services saved lives, and called on the prime minister to meet those affected by the cap. “Those that do sacrifice for our nation don’t just leave scars on the battlefield. They are left with scars for life, and understandably, they need help … and support from professionals,” he said.
